analysis.one_liner: Gives workers' unpaid wages and pension money priority over creditors in bankruptcy and restricts executive bonuses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The SLAP Act would rewrite bankruptcy rules so that workers come first when their employer goes broke. It doubles the amount of unpaid wages that get paid ahead of other creditors, removes the time limit on claiming back pay, and requires companies to keep paying into pension plans and withdrawal liability during bankruptcy instead of using the filing to escape those obligations. It also makes it much harder for a bankrupt company to hand out bonuses and retention pay to executives, extends the window for clawing back money improperly moved out of the company before a filing from two years to six, and requires judges weighing a sale of the company to consider which bidder keeps jobs and honors pension promises.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers file for bankruptcy. Today, unpaid wages are capped at $10,000 and only cover a 180-day window, and pension contributions rank behind other claims, so employees routinely eat the loss while lenders get paid. This bill doubles the wage cap to $20,000 with no time limit, elevates unpaid pension contributions and withdrawal liability to top-priority administrative expenses, forces companies to keep funding pensions through bankruptcy, and blocks courts from approving quick asset sales that leave pension obligations behind. It also protects workers indirectly by making it harder for insiders to extract bonuses and looted transfers before or during a case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees of bankrupt companies, especially pension-covered workers

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and strikes the 180-day time window, so longer-owed back pay and benefit contributions no longer get wiped out by the cap or the clock.

Elevates unpaid pension contributions and withdrawal liability to administrative expenses that must be paid in full ahead of ordinary creditors, and requires companies to keep satisfying minimum pension funding standards and making contributions even while in bankruptcy, closing the loophole where a filing freezes pension obligations.

Extends executive-pay restrictions to senior executive officers and the twenty next-most-highly paid employees or consultants, bans most bonuses and incentive pay during bankruptcy, and requires a court to find by clear and convincing evidence that any insider transfers are essential to the business and reasonable compared to peers, after accounting for wage concessions by nonmanagement workers.
Extends the look-back period for fraudulent transfers from two years to six years, giving courts more time to claw back money that was siphoned out of a company before it filed.

Restricts rushed asset sales: a trustee cannot sell substantially all of the company's property within 60 days of filing unless the court finds the value would otherwise collapse, and when judging competing bids the court must consider which bidder will keep existing jobs, preserve employment terms, and assume pension and retiree health obligations.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders, distressed-debt investors, and other creditors of bankrupt companies, who would recover less because workers' wages and pension contributions would be paid ahead of them; bankrupt companies' executives and insiders, who would lose easy access to retention bonuses, incentive pay, and insider transfers; and pension-withdrawing employers, who could no longer use a bankruptcy filing to escape multiemployer pension withdrawal liability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bankrupt companies' lenders, creditors, and executives

drawbacks.text: Requiring a company to keep fully funding its pension plans during bankruptcy could drain cash from a struggling firm and push it from reorganization into liquidation, which would destroy the very jobs and pensions the bill is meant to protect.

Because wages and pension contributions would jump ahead of lenders in the repayment line, creditors would likely charge more to lend to companies with underfunded pensions or unionized workforces, raising borrowing costs for exactly the firms the bill worries about.

The bill drew no cosponsors, including none from Manchin's own party, suggesting other senators viewed the changes as too sweeping even if sympathetic to the goal, and it never received a hearing or refinement in committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for workers are real and targeted at documented abuses of bankruptcy: capping wages while executives collect retention bonuses, and freezing pension funding while assets are sold off. But the bill was introduced as a statement piece rather than a negotiated bill, and its strongest provision — forcing continued full pension funding throughout bankruptcy — carries a genuine risk of hastening liquidations for the weakest companies. With no hearings, no cosponsors, and no committee markups, it was never refined to balance that tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the Stop Looting American Pensions Act on October 30, 2019, as a standalone bill to reorder bankruptcy priorities in favor of workers and pensions.
That same day the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held no hearing, took no vote, and never reported it out.

No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point — not a Democrat, not a Republican — and the bill attracted no floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing it under the rule that bills expire when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders, distressed-debt investors, and executives of bankrupt companies are better off, because the bankruptcy rules they use to get paid ahead of workers, freeze pension obligations, and collect bonuses while a company fails all remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bankruptcy lenders, distressed-debt investors, and executives

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it as the Senate's only vehicle for bankruptcy protections for wages and pensions; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat untouched from October 2019 until the Congress expired

against.name: Distressed-debt investors and bankruptcy lenders
against.role: Creditors whose recoveries would have been subordinated to wages and pension contributions
against.what_they_did: The bill's restructuring of claim priorities ran against the financial position of corporate creditors, who benefit from the existing bankruptcy hierarchy

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no partisan split can be measured; it had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no committee or floor action.

industries.note: These investors profit from the current bankruptcy hierarchy, under which their claims generally rank ahead of unpaid wages and pension contributions. The bill would have pushed workers' claims ahead of theirs and extended the window for clawing back pre-bankruptcy transfers, reducing recoveries.

industries.industry: Executives and insiders of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill extends bonus and retention-pay restrictions beyond insiders to the top paid officers and consultants, bans most incentive compensation during a case, and requires clear-and-convincing proof that any insider transfer is essential and reasonable. Today, bankrupt companies routinely win court approval of these payments while rank-and-file workers absorb cuts.

industries.industry: Multiemployer pension plans and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation
industries.note: Plans would collect unpaid contributions and withdrawal liability as top-priority claims, and the PBGC could enforce minimum funding standards without being blocked by the bankruptcy stay, keeping more money in pension funds and reducing calls on the federal pension backstop.

industries.industry: Private equity and quick-sale asset buyers
industries.note: The bill would bar selling substantially all of a company's assets in the first 60 days of a case unless the court finds the value is collapsing, and would require judges to favor bids that keep jobs and honor pension obligations over offers that strip assets and shed the workforce.
